memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "If you come across your enemy's ox or donkey wandering off, be sure to return it. If you see the donkey of someone who hates you fallen down under its load, do not leave it there; be sure you help them with it." - Exodus 23:4-5 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
What a remarkable command tucked into these ancient laws. If you find your enemy's animal wandering off, take it back to him. If the donkey of someone who hates you collapses under its load, do not walk past with satisfaction — stop and help. God calls His people to actively do good even to those who have wronged them. Long before Jesus taught it plainly, God was planting the seed: love your enemy.

This cuts against every natural instinct. When someone hates us, our flesh wants them to struggle, to fail, to feel the sting of their own trouble. To go out of our way to help them feels almost unnatural. But God calls us higher than our instincts. He asks us to break the cycle of hostility by choosing kindness where the world would choose revenge or indifference.

This is the very heart of the gospel. While we were still God's enemies, Christ died for us (Rom 5:10). God did not wait for us to become lovable; He loved us in our hostility and won us with kindness. And He calls us to reflect that same startling love. Jesus said it directly: love your enemies and do good to those who hate you (Luke 6:27). Is there an "enemy" whose fallen donkey God is asking you to help lift today?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
Is there someone who has wronged me that God is calling me to actively help?
How does the truth that Christ loved me as an enemy shape how I treat mine?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, You loved me while I was still Your enemy and won me with kindness. Give me grace to do good to those who have wronged me, breaking hostility with love. Amen.
